title: Turn a cake out onto a plate: clamp plate and pan together with both hands, turn them over and lift the pan off
instruction: Turn the cake out of its pan onto the plate, so that it ends up upside down on the plate on the stand with the pan off it.
context: Turning a freshly baked cake out of its tin is a step in nearly every home cake recipe, familiar to anyone who bakes at home, and it is done the same way in home kitchens and bakeries: a plate (or rack) goes upside down on the tin, both hands hold plate and tin together from opposite sides, and the two are turned over as one so the cake drops onto the plate; then the tin is lifted off (recipe writers describe the same hold-both-and-flip move, e.g. Alice Medrich's Food52 column on getting cakes out of their pans). Held from one side only, the stack hangs off that grip and comes apart, and the plate is far wider than one hand. The instruction states only the result.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. A fixed pale blue cake stand (a pedestal 13 cm across and 10 cm tall with a non-slip silicone top) stands 30 cm forward on the centre line. On it sits a round anodised-aluminium cake pan (about 1.9 mm sheet, 250 g): 14 cm across and 3.6 cm deep inside, with a flat rim 2.5 cm wide around its top (19.6 cm across) and two ears on the rim, 3 cm wide, reaching 13 cm from its centre towards each arm. In the pan is a baked sponge cake, 12.8 cm across and 2.8 cm tall (160 g), top up, with a dark crust on top. A flat white ABS plastic plate, 21 cm across and 6 mm thick (220 g), lies on the pan's rim, covering it. The pan, the cake and the plate are loose. Friction in the simulation (static / dynamic): pan and plate 0.6 / 0.5, cake 0.7 / 0.6, the stand's silicone top and the gripper pads 1.2 / 1.0. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Measured from the overhead and wrist videos and with a ruler and a protractor; partial credit is the best reached during the run. 1.0: the plate lies flat on the stand (its middle within 3 cm of the stand's), the cake lies on it upside down (crust down, turned more than 160 degrees) with its middle within 2.5 cm of the plate's, and the pan is off it (the pan's middle 13 cm or more from the cake's), all still for 2 s. 0.5: the cake lies on the plate on the stand like that, but the pan is still over it. 0.25: the cake has been turned upside down while off the table. 0.0: anything else.
reset_notes: Put the pan back on the stand, the cake in it crust up, and the plate on the pan's rim; nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.1, 20 Hz control) of a calibrated two-arm table. Simplified: the cake is a rigid disc (no crumbs, no sticking to the pan); the pan is one rigid body of a floor, 24 wall and 24 rim panels and two ears; friction is set per material (aluminium pan and ABS plate 0.6, sponge cake 0.7, silicone stand top 1.2). Dream-1 sees the 320 x 176 frames it expects; the demo video is rendered at 1280 x 720.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both arms lifted and turned in place near their starting positions; neither gripper reached the plate or the pan, and the stack stayed on the stand untouched); demo: 1.0
